description.purpose: The capability broker: a security boundary made of six cell types and no model. Three messages -- `access.request` -> `access.grant` -> `access.invoke`. An agent may ask in natural language; what travels on the wire is a HANDLE, and the secret never leaves the connector. `policy` decides deterministically (rules are ROWS, so politics is changed with an insert), `invoke` executes and resolves the address out of the GRANT, `sweep` and `clock` retire what expired. Two invariants carry the whole thing: the requester comes from the edge (R-AC-1) and the address comes from the grant (R-AC-2).
description.use_when: Once per member or per org level that owns credentials, as a sibling of the agents. Wire the lanes in the same mutation as the add_nodes, at the HIVE path -- never at a cell inside it. The broker is needed where an agent wants a NEW address or a NEW capability -- an answer inside a running conversation stays an ordinary reply edge (ruling L5), so this template is ADDITIVE and never sits in the hot path.
description.not_in_scope: No secret ON THE WIRE and no `secrets.db`: `./vault` holds the credentials, and the only path a plaintext one takes out of it is the injection at unlock into a connector named in `params.inject_map` -- never per request, never to an address a message could choose, and never back to whoever asked. `cred_refs` stays a catalogue of NAMES. No model anywhere -- nothing here asks one, and nothing here can. No approval lane in v1 (`require_approval` reports `pending` and mints nothing). And no enforcement of its own monopoly beyond the boundary: the substrate has no permission layer, so the broker is exactly as strong as the sentence `there is exactly one edge into the connector, and it comes from the access hive on the connect lane`.
examples: LANES - the hive path is the address and `hop.route` is the port; `params.ports` is empty, so no edge reaches a cell in here. in_request: an edge onto the HIVE carrying access.request as a tool_call turn and promoting the caller to context.requester -- a missing requester is a denial, not a default. in_invoke: the same, carrying access.invoke. grant: out of the hive on hop.route=='grant' -- a handle, never an address. ack: out on hop.route=='ack'. connect: out on hop.route=='connect' into the connector cell -- this MUST be the only edge that reaches it. error: out on hop.route=='error' into a drain the parent MUST wire.

THE VAULT - `./vault` is an interior cell and reachable from nowhere outside: the hive is sealed to its own path, so the port boundary refuses every edge into it from outside the scope. Its `params.broker` is `./invoke`; nobody else is answered at all. Secrets enter over the user channel only (`meclaw --vault /main/access/vault --vault-add <name>`), which writes straight into the cell's own database with no colony running -- so a credential never becomes a message. At unlock the vault hands each secret named in `params.inject_map` to its connector as a params update, once; the requester learns which name went where under which key, and never the value.

R-AC-1: a body claiming "requester":"agent:someone-else" changes nothing -- the field is never read, and the grant is issued to the identity the edge promoted. A body is model-writable; an edge is colony authority.
R-AC-2: a grant for one chat plus a payload naming another chat sends to the GRANT's chat, drops the key before the connector sees it, and records the attempt in the audit detail.

revocation without an update: one `revoked` row in grant_events, and the next invoke is refused although expires_at is still in the future -- the effective state is the newest event, read with order_by desc limit 1
the TTL: ./invoke compares expires_at on every call, ./sweep writes the `expired` row afterwards -- so the door closes on time even if the clock does not tick
a fresh instance grants nothing: every seeded policy row ships enabled 0, so the broker starts inert and an operator turns on exactly what they mean
